BOOK ENTRY
The covenant identity of a house, consisting of 3 things appointed and provided by its Head: the Word (the manna), the covenant law (the stone tables), and the fruitful priesthood (Aaron's budded rod). A counterfeit Name substitutes a different word, covenant, or priesthood; a Name is taken in vain when any one is rejected, replaced, or removed. A bride takes her Husband's Name by entering His house, coming under His authority, and obeying Him.

(2 Sam 6:2; 7:2, 13; 1 Kgs 8:20-21; Heb 9:4; Deut 8:3; 4:13; Num 17:5, 8; Ex 20:7; Isa 4:1) · see The Name, ch. 8

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

Nearly every Christian has ended a prayer with the words “in Jesus' Name.”
We do it because Jesus made a promise that sounds unlimited:

And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

Whatsoever is a hard word to explain away.
Many readers have prayed sincerely, attached the phrase exactly as they were taught, and received no answer.
If “in my Name” means adding the right words to the end, lived experience appears to contradict the promise.
The more honest conclusion is that something is missing from the usual definition.

A Name is not a magic phrase added to the end of a prayer.
It is not a pronunciation or sound, as though salvation depended on arranging the right syllables.
It is not merely a label pasted onto something while leaving the thing itself unchanged.

An answered prayer or a wonder would not rescue the incantation.
Jesus describes people who claim the greatest possible evidence:

Many will say to Me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in Your name, cast out demons in Your name, and done many wonders in Your name?
And then I will declare to them, I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness!

The testimony is theirs: “have we not?”
They thought they prophesied, cast out demons, and did wonders in His Name; Jesus never confirms that they acted in it.
He says He never knew them and identifies their actual deeds as lawlessness.

Even a sign that truly comes to pass does not settle whose Name is behind it.
Moses gave Israel that test before they entered the land:

If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder,
And the sign or the wonder come to pass, whereof he spake unto thee, saying, Let us go after other gods, which thou hast not known, and let us serve them;

Moses explains why God permits the sign: “the LORD your God is testing you to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 13:3, NKJV).
The test is resolved by the next command: “keep His commandments and obey His voice” (Deuteronomy 13:4, NKJV).
The wonder comes to pass, yet the prophet is false because his word leads away from obedience to God.
A miracle proves that something happened; it does not prove the Name claimed over it.
The Name on the lips must be tested against the Word, covenant, and authority the life obeys.

To discover what is missing, follow the Name where Scripture places it: over an ark, inside a house.
The ark is not empty.
It holds manna, stone tables, and a rod that has come alive.
Scripture defines each item in turn, and together they supply the substance no pronunciation or miracle can prove.

When David first brought the ark toward Jerusalem, Scripture joined the ark and the Name in a single description:

And David arose, and went with all the people that were with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from thence the ark of God, whose name is called by the name of the LORD of hosts that dwelleth between the cherubims.

The Name rests where the LORD dwells between the cherubim.
David later looks from his cedar house toward that ark still sheltered by curtains: “I dwell in an house of cedar, but the ark of God dwelleth within curtains” (2 Samuel 7:2).
God answers David's desire through his son: “He shall build an house for my name” (2 Samuel 7:13).

Solomon joins every term when the house is finished:

I am risen up in the room of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and have built an house for the name of the LORD God of Israel.
And I have set there a place for the ark, wherein is the covenant of the LORD, which he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.

David asks for a house for the ark.
God calls it a house for His Name.
Solomon builds the house for the Name and places the ark inside it.
The ark carries the substance of the Name, and the temple is the fixed house built around it.

Hebrews opens the ark and inventories its contents:

…the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant.

Exactly 3 things are named: manna, the tables of the covenant, and Aaron's fruitful rod.
Each has already been defined by Scripture.

The manna is the Word.
Moses says God fed Israel with manna “that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3).
The manna came as a daily portion of the Word, and God stated its purpose: “that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no” (Exodus 16:4).

The stone tables are the covenant law.
Moses does not ask us to infer it:

And he declared unto you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, even ten commandments; and he wrote them upon two tables of stone.

The covenant is spoken, commanded, and written.
When Moses came down the second time, he put those tables “in the ark which I had made; and there they be, as the LORD commanded me” (Deuteronomy 10:5).

Aaron's rod is the fruitful priesthood.
Korah's rebellion had challenged whom God appointed to draw near, so God required a rod from every tribal head and promised, “the man's rod, whom I shall choose, shall blossom” (Numbers 17:5).
The next morning the verdict was alive:

…behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.

The rod is authority appointed by God, and its fruit proves the priesthood God chose.
It was kept “before the testimony” as a witness against those who rejected that appointment (Numbers 17:10).

The ark therefore holds one coherent Name: the Head's Word, the Head's covenant, and the Head's appointed priesthood bearing fruit.
Remove any one and the object may keep its label, but it no longer carries the Name intact.

A Name is the covenant identity of a house.
The Head provides its Word, establishes its covenant law, and appoints its priesthood.
The house does not vote its head into existence or furnish him with a rival word.
It receives what its head provides.

God's answer to David turns on this double meaning of house.
David offers to build God a house of cedar; God replies, “the LORD telleth thee that he will make thee an house” (2 Samuel 7:11).
One house is a building; the other is a people descended from a head.
The Son of David joins them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up… he spake of the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21); “ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5); “Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we” (Hebrews 3:6).

Zechariah sees that Head as King and Priest together:

Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD… and he shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne.

The Name belongs to a house because a Name joins a head to a people under him.
This is why a wife is called by her husband's name.
Isaiah's 7 women ask one man, “only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach” (Isaiah 4:1).
They are asking for marriage, not a new pronunciation.

Scripture does not soften what entering that house means.
“The husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church… therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing” (Ephesians 5:23-24).
Peter points to Sarah as the pattern: “the holy women also, who trusted in God, adorned themselves, being in subjection unto their own husbands: even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord” (1 Peter 3:5-6).

The bride takes her Husband's Name by entering His house, coming under His authority, and obeying Him.
God describes His own marriage to Israel with the same covenant act: “I spread my skirt over thee… yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee… and thou becamest mine” (Ezekiel 16:8).
The covering is His wing. Its corners carry the tassels; when the wearer looks upon them, they remind him of all the LORD's commandments, to do them (Numbers 15:38-40).

This is also why a Name tells how its Head is known.
John gives the test without qualification:

And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments.
He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.

To know the Head is to receive His Word and keep His commandments.
A label detached from that substance makes Him unknown, which is why Jesus answers the loudest users of His Name, “I never knew you.”

Return to the promise that opened this chapter.
It cannot mean that any request becomes binding when the right sound is attached.
Paul extends the phrase over the whole life: “whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Colossians 3:17).
No one can pronounce a phrase over every breath and motion.
Everything can, however, be done within His priesthood, under His covenant, and in obedience to the Word of the Head whose Name is claimed.

John states the limit plainly: “if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us” (1 John 5:14).
To ask in His Name is to ask as one belonging to His house, in agreement with the will His Word reveals.
The opposite is equally plain: “He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination” (Proverbs 28:9).
The mouth may say the Name while the ear refuses what the Name carries.

Once a symbol is defined, it should unlock passages beyond the verses used to establish it.
The Lord's Prayer is the most familiar application of the Name's new meaning.
Read with the definition in place, its petitions gather the Word, covenant, priesthood, and obedient house into a single pattern:

Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.

“Hallowed be thy name” is not a compliment added before the requests.
It asks that the Name be made holy in the house that bears it.
Ezekiel gives the opposite and the remedy: Israel “profaned my holy name” among the nations when their conduct made the people of the LORD a reproach, and God promises, “I will sanctify my great name… when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes” (Ezekiel 36:20, 23).
The next petition explains how: “Thy will be done.”

The ark's contents then unfold through the prayer.
“Give us this day our daily bread” reaches back to the manna, the daily portion of the Word given to prove whether the people would walk in the law (Exodus 16:4).
The petition does not erase the request for literal food; it adds the deeper hunger for every Word from the mouth of God.

“Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” lives inside the covenant law.
The law commands the release of debt, “because it is called the LORD'S release” (Deuteronomy 15:2), and Luke places the meaning beside the image: “forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us” (Luke 11:4).
The one praying asks the covenant mercy he is commanded to practice.

The final plea, “deliver us from evil,” depends upon the priesthood.
Jesus shows that intercession when He tells Peter, “Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not” (Luke 22:31-32).
Our High Priest “ever liveth to make intercession” for those who come to God by Him (Hebrews 7:25).

The Lord's Prayer is therefore prayed in the Name from beginning to end: the Name hallowed in an obedient people, the Head's will done, His Word received as daily bread, His covenant mercy practiced, and His priestly intercession carrying the house through trial.
The symbol does more than correct a mistaken phrase at the end of prayer; it opens the prayer Jesus actually taught.

The third commandment now reaches farther than careless speech:

Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

Vain is emptiness, something reduced to nothing.
To take the Name in vain is to claim the covenant identity while rejecting, replacing, or removing the Word, the covenant law, or the fruitful priesthood appointed by its Head.
Willful disobedience empties the Name because it rejects the authority of the One whose Name is claimed.

Moses binds the Name directly to obedience: “observe to do all the words of this law… that thou mayest fear this glorious and fearful name” (Deuteronomy 28:58).
Ezekiel binds its profaning to the conduct of the people who wear it.
Jesus binds its empty use to lawlessness.
The witnesses agree: a Name becomes nothing when its substance is refused.

Isaiah makes the empty claim visible through a marriage proposal:

And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.

They want the man's Name while keeping their own bread and their own garment.
They ask for his covering without his provision, his household identity without submission to his house.
It is the marriage form of “Lord, Lord”: the Name claimed while the Head's Word and rule are refused.

A counterfeit Name does not merely miss one of the 3 pillars.
It supplies a different word, covenant, or priesthood and places them under another head.

Babel is the first organized attempt: “let us build us a city and a tower… and let us make us a name” (Genesis 11:4).
The next chapter gives the answer when God calls Abraham out and promises, “I will… make thy name great” (Genesis 12:2).
One Name is manufactured from below; the other is appointed and provided by the Head above.

The conflict ends on the forehead.
The beast marks its followers with “the name of the beast” (Revelation 13:17), while the Lamb stands with a people having His Father's “name written in their foreheads” (Revelation 14:1).
The Father's Name is not an empty inscription: the same vision identifies them as those who “keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus” (Revelation 14:12).

Every true Name has a Head, a Word, a covenant, a fruitful priesthood, and a house that bears them.
Every counterfeit replaces at least one of those with something appointed by another head.
This is why “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).
No other Head supplies the Word, covenant, and priesthood by which His house is saved.

The ark shows what the Name carries.
The house shows who bears it.
The bride shows how it is taken.
The life shows whether it is held in truth or in vain.

Who can bear such a Name without emptying it?
Isaiah frames the next question in one command: “seal the law among my disciples” (Isaiah 8:16).
What is a disciple, and what must be sealed within him?
